records.claim: Volcanism began 2.15 million years ago and proceeded through three major volcanic cycles.
records.passage: Volcanism began 2.15 million years ago and proceeded through three major volcanic cycles.

records.claim: The climactic eruption of the first and largest cycle produced the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff about 2.08 million years ago.
records.passage: The first-cycle caldera-forming event was the eruption of the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff at about 2.08 million years ago.

records.claim: The most recent supereruption, about 631,000 years ago, produced the Lava Creek Tuff and created the present Yellowstone Caldera.
records.passage: The most recent supereruption, about 631,000 years ago, produced the Lava Creek Tuff and created the present Yellowstone Caldera.

records.claim: Post-caldera eruptions included basalt flows, rhyolite domes and flows, with the last known magmatic eruption about 70,000 years ago.
records.passage: Post-caldera eruptions included basalt flows, rhyolite domes and flows, and minor explosive deposits, with the last known magmatic eruption about 70,000 years ago.

records.claim: The second cycle culminated in eruption of the Mesa Falls Tuff about 1.3 million years ago.
records.passage: The second cycle culminated in eruption of the Mesa Falls Tuff and formation of the Henry's Fork Caldera about 1.3 million years ago.

narration.text: Yellowstone erupted 631,000 years ago. Is it overdue?
Three caldera-forming eruptions in about 2.1 million years.
Its last magmatic eruption of any kind was 70,000 years ago.
A new supereruption would bury nearby states in ash.
Far downwind, ash would ground flights and smother crops.
But eruptions don't run on a schedule, so it isn't overdue.
Smaller lava flows are far likelier than another giant blast.
So Yellowstone's real risk is disruption, not extinction.
